approachQuestion.prompt: A designer chooses nonnegative integer heights b[i] beneath nonnegative integer caps a[i]. Require a peak position p such that b[0]≤...≤b[p] and b[p]≥...≥b[n-1]; plateaus are allowed. Every b[i] must be at most a[i]. Return the greatest possible sum of chosen heights, without constructing them. Caps are at most 1,000,000. Example: [3,1,4,2] returns 8, using [1,1,4,2]. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The input is immutable; n is between 1 and 200,000. All integers, indices, counts, and arithmetic results fit in signed 64-bit machine words; comparisons and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Compute L[i], the best sum from 0 through i when i is a peak for that prefix. With an increasing stack, pop caps greater than a[i]; let j be the surviving top. Set L[i]=a[i]×(i-j)+L[j], or a[i]×(i+1) if absent. Compute symmetric R[i] from the right. Return max over i of L[i]+R[i]-a[i].
options.feedback: For a fixed peak i, each left height is the minimum cap from that position through i; the right side is symmetric. The nearest non-greater cap lets a block share the current cap, while the earlier optimal slope is reused. Subtracting a[i] counts the peak once.

options.text: Return the sum of caps because choosing b=a always maximizes the sum.
options.feedback: Caps can contain a valley with rises on both sides. For [3,1,3], b=a is not a permitted mountain; the optimum is 5, not 7.

options.text: Choose the first position with the largest cap as the peak, greedily lower heights outward, and return that sum.
options.feedback: The tallest cap need not be the best peak. For [5,1,4,4], a peak at 0 gives 8, while a peak at 2 or 3 gives 10.

options.text: For each possible peak, set it to its cap and move outward in both directions taking min(cap, previous chosen height); sum the result and keep the best.
options.feedback: This is correct but rescans most of the array for each peak, creating quadratic work. Directional stack totals reuse those slope sums.

feedback.reason: Compute optimal capped slope totals using nearest non-greater boundaries and combine two directional contributions.
details: Build optimal left-slope sums using an increasing cap stack and reuse the sum before the nearest non-greater cap. Repeat symmetrically for right-slope sums. For each peak combine its two sums, subtract its cap once, and maximize.

For a fixed peak, every outward height is capped by the smallest cap passed so far. Directional slope sums summarize those clipped choices. Subtract the peak once when joining left and right, since both sums include it.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For two-slope-stack-totals, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the number of caps. Allocate two sum arrays and a reused index stack, with scalar arithmetic only; no candidate mountain is copied.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Two monotone-stack sum passes and one peak scan use linear work and arrays.
details: Each directional slope-sum pass inserts an index once and removes it at most once, so both passes and the final peak comparison total O(n). The left/right sum arrays and working cap stack use O(n) auxiliary space. Rebuilding all slopes independently per peak would be quadratic, but the stored summaries avoid it.
